## Abstract

## Introduction

Hepatitis C virus causes chronic liver morbidity and mortality. While global HCV burden has improved in recent years, incidence continues to rise [@bai_global_2025]. In 2013, viral hepatitis represented the seventh greatest cause of mortality globally, with approximately 1.4 million deaths due to acute cases, cirrhosis, and liver cancer. Nearly half of these deaths are attributed to HCV. Among people living with HIV, coinfections with HCV are common, with approximately 2.9 million cases reported [@OrganisationMondialeSante; @VIHSidaHepatite2025]. At the global scale, 50 million people are estimated to be living with HCV, with approximately 1 million new cases annually.

Acute HCV infections are generally asymptomatic and rarely fatal. Approximately 30% of people infected spontaneously eliminate the virus in the six months following infection, while 70% develop chronic infection. Among those with chronic infections, the risk of developing cirrhosis within 20 years is between 15-30% [@Hepatitisb]. No vaccine is currently available against HCV, but direct acting antivirals prompt viral elimination in 95% of treated patients. However, access to diagnostics and treatment remain limited [@Hepatitisa; @Hepatitisb].

In West Africa, between 10 to 33 million people are infected with HCV, which is responsible for 10 to 25% of liver cancers [@linganiChangingEpidemiologyHepatitis2020]. Burkina Faso has intermediate to elevated HCV burden, with approximately 720,000 people living with chronic infection. Each year, nearly 900 deaths are attributed to HCV complications. A national study conducted in 2010 reported seroprevalence of 3.6% in the general population, with a particularly elevated prevalence of 13.2% in the southwestern region of Djôrô, suggesting an active epidemic in the region [@medaHepatitisVirusSeroprevalence2018]. In this context, we conducted a study in 2020 to improve our understanding of HCV at the household level and identify factors explaining this high prevalence. HCV case clusters were observed within households, raising the possibility of intrafamilial transmission. In this study, we investigate HCV transmission at the household level using phylogenetic analysis of HCV sequence data.

HCV is an enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus of the family Hepacivirus. Its two envelope glycoproteins (E1 and E2) facilitate attachment and penetration of hepatocytes. The core and NS5B protein-coding regions of its genome are the most common sequencing targets.

HCV has been characterized into eight distinct genotypes, and over 100 subtypes, differentiated by geographical, epidemiological, and clinical characteristics. [@chevaliezVirusLhepatiteVHC,@FlaviviridaeClassificationLHepacivirus].Genotypes 1,2, and 3 are globally widespread, while genotypes 5 and 6 are more commonly found in southern Africa and southeast Asia. Genotype 4 is predominant in central and north Africa, while genotypes 1 and 2 are more dominant in west Africa [@zebaCharacterisationHepatitisVirus2014].

New infections typically occur in high-risk populations, such as injection drug users (IDU), men who have sex with men (MSM), and sex workers (SW). In Sub-Saharan Africa, transmission occurs through iatrogenic sources, vertical transmission (mother-to-child), sexual practices involving exposure to blood, and social practices such as piercing, scarification, and tattooing [@ouobaEpidemiologicProfileHepatitis2021, @Hepatitisb].

### Viral diversity of HCV Strains

As with other RNA viruses, HCV has a high mutation rate, estimated at $10^{-3}$ substitutions per site per year, contributing to its high genetic variability. Several closely related yet distinct HCV populations (referred to as quasispecies) can be found within a single infected patient [@pawlotskyVirusLhepatite2002, @mennecierVirusLhepatiteMonhepatogastro2022].

### Households

In statistical terms, a household is a group of people who habitually live in the same dwelling, regardless of whether or not they are related [@MenageInsee]. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Demography (INSD) of Burkina Faso, a household is the basic unit used in statistical surveys. It refers to a group of people (whether related or not) who live in the same dwelling, pool their resources, and collectively meet their essential needs. A household may consist of a single person or several individuals; for example, a head of household, his wife or wives, his unmarried children, and/or other people living together [@BurkinaFasoRecensement]. Household transmission may occur through vertical transmission, transmission between sexual partners within the household, or contaminated objects such as knives, razors, or toothbrushes.

## Methods

The ANRS REVERSO study was conducted in 2020 in the southwest region of Djôrô, Burkina Faso.

Testing for HCV was conducted using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) during household visits. We consider households in which we observe at least two cases of HCV infection as a household HCV cluster.

Among participants who tested positive by RDT, dried blood spot (DBS) samples were collected (via fingerprick among adults and children over two years, and from heels of children under two years) and preserved on Whatman 903 Proteinsaver Cards (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany).

To detect and quantify HCV RNA in these samples, we used the Cobas AmpliPrep/Cobas TaqMan (qPCR) test. We conducted RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing for core and NS5B genome regions. We cleaned and trimmed Sanger sequence results using a Phred score threshold $Q \ge 20$. Residual ambiguous bases (N) were corrected by consulting the raw chromatogram signals at the positions of the actual peaks. The primary sequence was defined based on the highest fluorescent signal at each site, while the secondary sequence was defined based on the second strongest signal, using a detection threshold of 25% of the primary signal. A consensus sequence was generated by combining the primary and secondary sequences according to the IUPAC code nomenclature, which allows for the capture of positions exhibiting a detectable heterogeneous viral population (quasispecies diversity). Primary, secondary, and consensus sequences were concatenated for multiple sequence alignment and phylogenetic analysis.

## Intrahost HCV Genetic Heterogeneity

To study intra-host genetic heterogeneity, the consensus sequences from both groups (cases and controls) were used to determine the number of ambiguous nucleotide sites in each sequence. Viral diversity ratios (VDRs) were calculated using the formula below:

$$ \text{Viral Diversity Ratio} = \frac{\text{Number of ambiguous sites}} {\text{Sequence Length (BP)}} \times 100 $$ We calculated median and interquartile range (IQR) of VDRs within the entire study population and among individuals belonging to the same household. Viral diversity between the two groups was compared using the Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

For consensus sequences from households, we formulated hypotheses regarding HCV transmission events. We assumed that, for an infected individual within a household, transmission could have occurred either inside or outside the household. Based on genetic distances, a household of two infected individuals was considered to correspond to one transmission event, while a household of three individuals corresponded to three transmission events. These transmission events were then plotted graphically.

To determine whether infection occurred within or between households, an overall genetic distance threshold was defined based on the median genetic distances of the control group, along with the 5th and 75th percentiles, which served as reference intervals. A genetic distance threshold of 3%, based on the literature, was used to identify probable within-household transmissions. Thus, transmission events with a genetic distance of less than 3% were considered probable within-household transmissions; those between the 3rd and 5th percentiles as low to moderate genetic proximity transmissions; those between the 5th percentile and the median as moderate divergences; and those above the 75th percentile were considered between-household transmissions.

Multiple alignment was performed using MAFFT (version 7.526) with automated alignment strategy selection. To estimate genetic distance within household, we used the Neighbor-Joining (NJ) method (@saitou_neighbor-joining_1987). We also used the Tamura-Nei substitution model (\@tamura_estimation_1993) to account for differences in transition and transversion rates, as well as unequal frequencies of nucleotide bases and branch lengths. This model includes several parameters: base frequencies (3 independent parameters), substitution rates (2 parameters), and branch lengths, totaling 2N - 3 parameters for an unrooted tree. In total, the model comprises 2N + 2 parameters, where N corresponds to the number of sequences (or terminal leaves). The pairwise genetic distance matrix was calculated in R (version 4.6.0) using the dist.dna() function, employing the TN93 model with pairwise gap removal. Distances were calculated for all sequence pairs, resulting in 2 comparisons, and then classified into two categories: intra-household distances (between individuals within the same household) and inter-household distances (between individuals from different households).

The selection of the best nucleotide substitution model was performed in R (version 4.6) using the modelTest() function from the phangorn package (version 2.12.1), comparing the JC69, HKY85, TN93, and GTR models, with and without gamma distribution (+G) and proportion of invariant sites (+I), according to the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). The model with the lowest AIC value was selected.

The phylogenetic tree was then reconstructed using maximum likelihood (ML) with RAxML. If the model selected by R differed from the models directly available in RAxML, we defaulted to the GTR+G (GTRGAMMA) or GTR+G+I (GTRGAMMAI) model, which corresponds to the approximation compatible with the model selected by phangorn. The topological robustness of the tree was evaluated using 1,000 bootstrap replicates.

We described the sociodemographic data (age, sex, relationship to the head of household, etc.) for both groups (control and household). Age was described using the median and interquartile range (IQR). The significance of the difference between intra- and inter-family distance was tested using the Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon signed-rank test). To represent the matrix of genetic distances between viral sequences from household clusters, a heatmap was used to visualize the genetic distances between each pair of sequences. In this representation, each cell corresponding to the genetic distance between the (CONSENSUS OR PRIMARY SEQUENCES?) of two individuals. Light colors reflect a low genetic distance, while dark colors indicate a higher genetic distance. The diagonal line represents a comparison of an individual with itself, and therefore the distance is zero.

## Results

For this study, a total of 510 households were surveyed, 179 of which had at least one positive HCV case. Among these, 85 households had at least two HCV cases within the same household and were considered household clusters. From these household clusters, 30 participants were selected for Sanger sequencing. Of the 30 samples, 25 were successfully amplified for the NS5B region. Among these, 18 were of HCV genotype 2. These 18 sequences came from participants across 8 household clusters.

Among the control population (individuals in non-household clusters), a total of 80 samples were selected, 51 of which were amplified for the NS5B region. Of these 51 samples, 47 belonged to genotype 2.

The median age of participants in the household cluster group was 40 years with an interquartile range (IQR) of \[18-57.5\] years, and 38.89% were female. In the control group, the median age was 44 years with an IQR of \[31-60\] years, and 59.57% were female (Table \ref{tab: characteristics}).

In the household cluster group, HCV intra-host VDR ranged from 0 to 24.29% (median 16.50%; IQR \[0.97-18.45\]). Households M01 (18.15 IQR\[18.03-18.26\]), M02 (18.99 IQR\[18.57-19.87\]), M07 (15.15 IQR\[13.48-16.81\]) and M08 (19.69 IQR\[17.39-21.99\]) showed high levels of diversity among participants, while households M03 (0.64 IQR\[0.48-0.80\]) and M04 (0 IQR\[0-0\]) were characterized by a low proportion of ambiguous sites, reflecting more homogeneous viral populations. In contrast, households M05 (10.63 IQR\[6.75-14.50\]) and M06 (1 IQR\[0.50-10.38\]) showed greater variability among their members (figure \~\ref{fig:DVF}).

In the control group, the ratio of intra-host diversity ranged from 0.31 to 11.36% (median 1.86%; IQR \[0.95-2.90\]), suggesting a more homogeneous viral population and low heterogeneity of HCV viral diversity. (figure \~\ref{fig:DVC}).

We found a tatistically significant difference in intra-host diversity of HCV between groups (p=0.02) (figure \~\ref{fig:compare}).

Overall, the genetic distance ranged from 0 to 0.39 (median 0.18; IQR 0.13–0.26). In the household cluster group, it ranged from 0 to 0.31; IQR 0.05–0.13), reflecting greater genetic homogeneity of the viral sequences. Conversely, in the control group, the genetic distance ranged from 0.01 to 0.38 (median 0.24; IQR 0.17–0.28), indicating higher genetic diversity among individual infected households than multiply infected households. Comparison between the two groups using the Wilcoxon test showed a statistically significant difference (p \< 0.05).

In total, the 18 sequences from household clusters allowed for 153 genetic distance comparisons, including 12 intra-household comparisons and 141 inter-household comparisons. The inter-household genetic distances had a median of 0.22 \[IQR 0.14–0.26\], while the intra-household distances had a median of 0.19 \[IQR 0.03–0.28\]. Although the intra-household distances were slightly smaller, the comparison between the two distributions using the Wilcoxon/Mann-Whitney test did not reveal a statistically significant difference (p = 0.34) (Figure \~\ref{fig:compare2}).

From the heatmap, we observe that two individuals of M06 (intra), M04, and M06 (inter) have a very low genetic distance (approximately 0). Furthermore, the observed genetic distance between M02-2110425 and M06-3322291 (inter-household) is very low (0.0096), indicating a high similarity between the two viral sequences and a marked phylogenetic proximity (figure \~\ref{fig:matrice}).

Analysis of household transmission events shows that some households, notably M01, M02, and one individual from M06, exhibit genetic distances below the 3% threshold, suggesting a high degree of phylogenetic proximity of viral sequences and probable intra-household transmission. The genetic distances observed in households M05, the two individuals from M06, M07, and M08, falling between the 3% threshold and the 5th percentile, are within a range of low to moderate genetic proximity, remaining consistent with significant viral similarity. For household M04, whose VDR lies between the 5th percentile and the median, the genetic distance reflects a moderate divergence. In contrast, household M03, characterized by a higher distance, suggests a less genetic proximity of viral sequences, which is less compatible with intra-household transmission and could reflect a distinct origin of infections or an unidentified common source (figure \~\ref{fig:evenemt}).

Phylogenetic analysis of household clusters, performed using the distance method and the Maximum Likelihood method, reveals partial clustering of sequences belonging to the same household, suggesting significant genetic proximity within certain households. In particular, households M02 and M06 exhibit tighter clustering of their viral sequences, consistent with close genetic proximity and possible intra-household transmission. Conversely, other households, such as M03, M05, M07, and M08, show a more pronounced dispersion of sequences, suggesting greater genetic heterogeneity and less evident transmission (Figure \~\ref{fig:foyerM}).

The phylogeny inferred by Maximum Likelihood is generally similar to that obtained by the distance method. Several clades are well supported by bootstrap values ​​between 74% and 100%, which strengthens the robustness of certain groupings. In particular, the clade comprising several household sequences (M01, M02, M03, M05, and M06) shows maximum support (bootstrap = 100%). Another grouping, such as M05-3322241 and M06-3322292, is strongly supported (bootstrap = 98%), while their grouping with the sequence M04-3312412 shows 93% support. However, we observe in the tree that sequences originating from the same household do not strictly cluster within the same exclusive monophyletic clade (figure \~\ref{fig:foyerML}), thus limiting the conclusion of intra-household transmission.

Phylogenetic analysis integrating the sequences of the household clusters and the control group using the distance method (Figure \~\ref{fig:Fcontrole}) shows that the sequences of household clusters do not form a cluster entirely distinct from the control group. The sequences of the individual households M04, M05, and M06 consistently form the same clade, suggesting a genetic proximity consistent with shared viral circulation within households (M06), while others are more dispersed and closer to sequences of the control group.

The phylogenetic tree obtained using the maximum likelihood method highlights several well-supported clades, with bootstrap values ​​ranging from 78% to 100%. In this tree, sequences from different households are not distributed according to strictly separate clades, and sequences belonging to the same households do not systematically form monophyletic clades. However, a grouping of the two sequences from household M06 is observed, as well as a grouping between a sequence from households M04 and M05, with a bootstrap value of 78%, indicating moderate support for this clade (figure \~\ref{fig:FcontroleML}).

## Discussion

Most HCV sequences in our study were identified as genotype 2, which is particularly relevant in the context of this study as it is the most prevalent in West Africa \[CITATION\].

Analysis of intra-host HCV viral diversity in household clusters reveals a median of 16.50% (IQR: \[0.97–18.45\]), reflecting strong heterogeneity between individuals. Certain households, in particular M05 and M06, present very marked variability between their members, which could reflect distinct evolutionary dynamics or different infection durations (figure \ref{fig:DVF}). Conversely, the control group displays a lower median, of 1.86% (IIQ: \[0.95–2.90\]), with more homogeneous intra-host diversity and low heterogeneity of HCV viral diversity. This observation could be linked to a more recent infection or to specific transmission dynamics.

Phylogenetic analysis of HCV showed significantly lower median genetic distance within than between households. Furthermore, examination of the distance matrix revealed low genetic distances between certain individuals from the same household, in particular within household M06, as well as between individuals from different households (figure \ref{fig:matrix}). These observations may reflect intra-household transmission, a common source of infection, shared circulation of viral strains or even transmissions between households. However, these results alone do not allow us to conclude that there is overall intra-household transmission in all household clusters.

Furthermore, according to both distance and maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees, sequences from the same homes did not form monophyletic groups (clusters). Only the two sequences of M06 and sometimes the two sequences of M02 formed clades, but we cannot confirm intra-familial transmission from these results. Our results suggest a high level of heterogeneity of genetic profiles both between and within households.

However, our study has certain limitations. First of all, the number of household clusters included in the analysis is low: only two households had three sequences, while the others had only two. This limited sample size may partly explain the results obtained. Furthermore, Sanger sequencing underestimates the diversity of HCV quasi-species and is not the most suitable approach for molecular epidemiology studies of HCV, in particular for the analysis of transmission clusters.

### Conclusion

Ultimately, this study allowed the application of molecular epidemiology to the investigation of household HCV transmission. The analyses performed show that the presence of several cases in the same household does not necessarily imply household transmission. The absence of strict monophyletic clades in all the households studied does not allow us to conclude that there was household transmission in all cases. Nevertheless, certain phylogenetic clusters were identified in some households, suggesting a degree of genetic similarity between certain viral strains shared within households. These observations suggest that several infections were likely acquired outside the family setting, possibly linked to iatrogenic or community-acquired factors, or other modes of transmission.
